body.text: Pressure is growing on the global steel industry to replace coal-based production with low-emission alternatives. Green iron, produced using renewable electricity and hydrogen instead of metallurgical coal, will be critical for decarbonisation. This transition will have far-reaching economic and geopolitical consequences, creating opportunities for potential exporters such as Australia. Yet far less attention has been paid to what this emerging trade, and greater reliance on imported green iron, would mean for potential importers.
Australia needs to accelerate green iron production rather than rely indefinitely on gas. Policy efforts should focus on overcoming the cost barriers to genuinely green production.

Australia has strong fundamentals to be a key player in future green iron trade, with abundant renewable energy resources, extensive iron ore reserves, and long-established trading relationships with the major steel-producing economies in East Asia. These advantages could support substantial green iron exports. Capitalising on this opportunity, however, will require understanding the importer side of the equation.

An Australia-East Asia trade corridor is at the centre of discussions about the future of green iron. China, the world’s largest iron ore importer and Australia’s biggest customer, also has sizeable domestic iron ore resources, a growing supply of steel scrap, and vast renewable energy capacity. Therefore, how the transition to green iron reshapes its trading relationship with Australia is a complex question. South Korea and Japan, meanwhile, have globally competitive steel industries but face constraints. It is much harder for them to produce renewable energy and green hydrogen at the scale and cost required to domestically produce green iron. These countries will therefore likely have to import a share of green iron needs.

For potential importing countries, the question is not simply where to buy low-emission iron. It is how to decarbonise one of their most important industries while preserving industrial competitiveness. This question is particularly consequential for South Korea, where the steel industry is deeply integrated with its major industries such as automotive manufacturing, construction, and shipbuilding. Shifting the upstream ironmaking process overseas would have consequences far beyond the steel industry itself, affecting supply chain resilience and industrial capabilities. Part of the equation lies in economic implications tied to jobs in key Korean manufacturing hubs. Another concern is geopolitical. Echoing recent energy supply shocks following the Strait of Hormuz crisis, offshoring a certain part of production brings reliance on foreign trade partners and exposes these supply chains to disruptions, which can impact key downstream sectors. To make the supply chain security and jobs sacrifice worthwhile requires a convincing trade-off.

Imported green iron could nevertheless play a significant role, particularly if Australia can turn its abundant renewable resources into a cost advantage. The high cost of renewable hydrogen and the investment required for new facilities make this difficult. Yet there is no guarantee that Australia’s potential advantage will last. Policy support and investment in importing countries could make domestic green iron production more competitive, narrowing Australia’s advantage.

Speed and cost will be critical to capitalising on Australia’s window of opportunity. It must establish a credible, cheaper supply of green iron before importing countries develop stronger alternatives at home that reduce the incentive for offshoring. However, another factor is even more critical for long-term competitiveness – whether the supply Australia brings to market will be genuinely green.

Australia’s prospective advantage lies in combining abundant renewable energy with extensive iron ore reserves to produce low-emission iron. Yet this fundamental rationale is becoming increasingly blurred by projects that plan to begin with natural gas-based direct reduced iron (DRI) and switch to green hydrogen at some later stage.
This open-ended gas-first strategy is difficult to reconcile with Australia’s ambition to become a green iron exporter.

This open-ended gas-first strategy is difficult to reconcile with Australia’s ambition to become a green iron exporter. Although starting with gas may lower initial costs, it risks sacrificing long-term competitiveness. Gas-based DRI remains dependent on fossil fuels and cannot deliver the depth of emissions reductions that importing countries will ultimately require. It also risks locking in carbon-intensive infrastructure, prolonging fossil fuel dependence and delaying the transition to hydrogen produced with renewable electricity.

For Korean steelmakers, importing gas-based DRI would provide only a partial answer to their decarbonisation challenge. As carbon standards tighten, the value of imported iron will increasingly depend on its actual carbon intensity rather than promises that it may become greener later. The strategic case for offshoring weakens if it cannot provide a genuinely green alternative, particularly given the trade-offs for supply chain resilience and industrial capabilities.

Australia therefore needs to accelerate green iron production rather than rely indefinitely on gas. Policy efforts should focus on overcoming the cost barriers to genuinely green production. Australia’s legitimacy as a green iron producer will depend on whether it delivers what the name promises: a supply chain that ultimately achieves steel production without coal, and without another fossil fuel taking its place.
Yeongmin Kweon is a researcher at Solutions for Our Climate (SFOC), where he focuses on reducing carbon emissions in South Korea's steel industry.
